```{r}
source("R/helpers.R")
set.seed(STUDENT_SEED)

rate <- 1
population_mean <- 1 / rate
population_sd <- 1 / rate
generator <- function(sample_size) {
  rexp(sample_size, rate = rate)
}
```

## Question and prediction

The Exponential population is continuous and strongly right-skewed. I expect
its sample means to need more observations than the Standard Normal or die
population before the shape looks approximately normal.

For an Exponential distribution with rate 1, the theoretical mean and standard
deviation are both 1.

## Original population

```{r}
population <- rexp(10000, rate = rate)
plot_population_histogram(population, "Original Exponential population", "Population value")
```

The long right tail is the main feature that may slow the convergence of the
sampling distribution.

## Simulation and theoretical comparison

```{r}
means_by_size <- simulate_sample_means(generator)
summary_table <- summarize_sample_means(
  means_by_size,
  theoretical_mean = population_mean,
  theoretical_sd = population_sd
)
print_summary(summary_table)
first_screened_n <- summary_table$sample_size[summary_table$screening_rule][1]
chosen_row <- summary_table[summary_table$sample_size == first_screened_n, , drop = FALSE]
```

## Sample sizes investigated

I investigated sample sizes `n = 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200`. I used
small values to show the initial right skew and larger values to see how much
the long tail slowed the approach to normality. I included `n = 30` because it
is a common classroom rule, but I did not assume it would work here.

The theoretical standard error is `1 / sqrt(n)`. I compare it with the
simulated standard deviation of the sample means.

## Visual evidence

```{r}
selected_sizes <- c(5, 20, 50, 200)
plot_selected_diagnostics(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Exponential")
plot_selected_qq(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Exponential Q-Q plot")
```

I expect the smaller sample sizes to retain some right skew. At larger sample
sizes, the center should become more symmetric, although the tails may still
show departures from a perfect normal line.

## Approximate normal decision

My final answer is **n =** `r first_screened_n`. At this sample size, the
histogram was much more balanced, and the Q-Q plot was more nearly straight
than it was for the smaller sample sizes. The skewness was
`r round(chosen_row$skewness, 3)`, the excess kurtosis was
`r round(chosen_row$excess_kurtosis, 3)`, and the simulated standard deviation
was `r round(chosen_row$simulated_sd, 4)` compared with a theoretical standard
error of `r round(chosen_row$theoretical_se, 4)`.

The smaller sample sizes still showed right skew. The first reasonable value
was much larger than the value for the Normal population because the original
Exponential distribution has a long right tail.

## What surprised me

I was surprised that the Exponential distribution needed a much larger sample
size than the Normal population. The standard error matched the theoretical
formula well, but the shape still took longer to look normal.
